blocks.x: What's your full name? My full name? David Williams Jr. David Williams Jr. Dave A. Williams Jr. That's my full name. And what was your father's name? Dave Williams Sr. What's the A for? Albert. Oh, okay. Let's see, today's date is March the... What's today's date? March the... 20... 20... 28th. 1974. Okay. And we're at the Archive of New Honest Jazz, and we've been listening to these tapes. How did you happen to make this recording session with Poorey? Poorey? Yeah, that one we just prepared.

Oh, well, we were working. I had a little band at the time. Poorey was working with me, and those, some of the things that we did, were original, some of my things. Mm-hmm. Quick? Yeah. Oh, we happened to, you know, we got together, did those things. We had a little company, a little small company was named Eagle.
Where's the company from?
Company right out here in New Orleans.
Who owned it?
Yeah. Right, right down, they call it, Little Woods down there, going out toward the lake.
Oh, yeah. Who was the guy? Who was the guy that owned it?
Uh, Janellis. Janellis. Janellis. Who was his name? Janellis, yeah. We never did do anything with the numbers. Poor fella died before we got a chance to do anything. Yeah.
I want to tell them about what happened to those records. Yeah. When the guy died and everything. Or why he died. What happened?

Oh, well, we did the recording, and before we could release the things, he died. I mean, I think that was good. I think that was during the time, Bessie, that storm came up there, and just straw, you know, plenty of different things he had, little property and all that. And after that, the man, wife quit him and everything. And when I heard from McGinney was dead.
Yeah. Now, uh, Clive, what's your name, anyway? I just want to see if he's picking you up.
Clive Wilson.
Okay. Let me move it over a little closer to you. Okay. Yeah, your name is Clive what? Clive Wilson.
Clive Wilson.
Okay. Yeah. I guess it's good. All right. Now, uh, where did you make that session, though? What studio did you, or in a home or what? Home with Paul Reilly.
Oh, with Paul Reilly, we made that section in a home, in a house. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Who's? Down in Lowood. Janellis.
Oh, Janellis, that's what I'm saying. And, oh, what did he do? Was he having another business or something?

Well, I don't know what he, I know he was very interested in, he was interested in talents. He, uh, he was very interested in me and he always thought that I should have gotten a break in this field. And, and we've been friends a while and he always told me if you ever get a chance, you're on record. And somehow he, he happened to get his own little, little labor. He had a labor. And, uh, so we went on and got together and recorded.
Did they have anybody else on the ego label?

Or any other group like? Yeah. I don't know. I never, I never really knew did he ever do anything. I think I was the first one and after that, that was it. I believe. I'm not quite sure. Who was there?
During the section?

Mm-hmm. Well, the president at the local during that time, Lewis Contrell, and the boy that did the section was Lord Washington, Poirier, and myself and, uh, who was that fellow, that bass player, man? Uh, uh, uh, Kimball. Norvin Kimball. Norvin Kimball. Norvin Kimball, yeah.
Uh, what did Lloyd do?
Lloyd played drumming on the section.
How did it happen he was playing drums then?

Uh, what happened that, we had a little group at the, uh, Lamp Post on Bourbon and the Sinan, right across from Pete Fountain Place, and, uh, we was, uh, Lori and I was working together. You know you'd like to do the ink spot thing. Mm-hmm. And, uh, so we just had a piano, just me on piano, so we decided to try to fully in a little mode. We couldn't do ink spot numbers all night long. It got monotonous. So I had Lloyd, Lloyd rented an old drum. And so Lloyd started playing drums along with me. And then after that, then, business pick up kind of good. Then the fellas told me to get a few more pieces. That's how I ate it on Kilman Puri. And kept Lloyd playing drums.
You know, I never did know that Lloyd was a drummer before that. I don't remember playing that.
Well, Lloyd wasn't. I never remember Lloyd being a drummer myself before that.
No. He just picked it up.
Yeah. Just happened to pick it up. Played real nice time, too.
Yeah. Did you do all those, make up all those numbers yourself?
Yes, I made those numbers.
Oh, uh, did that guy have anybody else there at the session? Did he have his, who was the engineer? I forgot to ask you that.
He was the engineer. Yeah? Yeah. He had his little machine that sit up. He did it himself, right in his front room.
And it was his wife or children or anybody around?
Well, yeah. His wife was around.
So, it was just like being at home or something? Yeah, just like being at home. Did you get your kicks?
I got plenty of kicks, man. Yeah. Everybody got the kicks at the little section. They were real nice. So, I'm sorry that nothing could have happened with the numbers. So, we're here trying again.
Yeah. You know, when I went in there sometime, Willie Humphrey would be there with you. Do you remember that?

Well, I'm happy to play some chimes, which I mean he wouldn't ever mention that he played with such a small musician like me, you know. Many of them wouldn't. Yeah, but I was there. I remember. Yeah, but I know you know. Just like, you remember when I was working for Leroy, the first patio out in there on Boyfriend Street? Mm-hmm. And I had Frog, Tramore Man, Frog. I had Jack Willis. I have Kimball, the big clarinet player that died there. Sam Dutre. And all those boys working with me. But right now, they wouldn't even mention that they worked with a small fry like me. Yeah, during that time, I had those people working with me. Did you ever know George Williams? We worked a long time.
Are you any kin to George Williams? No, I'm not kin to George Williams. Did you ever know him?

The drummer George Williams? Yeah. Sure, I know George. Good. I worked with George. I worked in George Band. During the time him and Poirier worked together. And we worked at that same plate that he called the Blue Angel on Boyfriend Street in the 200 block. Long time ago. Long time ago. I worked with George. George and Poirier? George and Poirier. And who else? Do you remember? I don't remember. I can't recall.
And did George ever work in your band? No, George never worked in my band. Not regular. No.

Did you ever know Blanche Thomas? Blanche Thomas was vocal with my group. Where? At Leroy Place. During the time I was just telling this now about Frog and Jack and them working with me. But Blanche was working during the time with us. Yeah, she was vocal during the time.
Was there a place called the Playhouse or the Playboy or something like that around?

Yeah. Yeah, I played the, I think with the, not the Playboy, I think with the, the Playhouse I used to work at on, I think it was St. Louis and Bourbon. And me and Bob Ostens, another good musician, Harold. What does Harold play? Harold played saxophone.
Harold Batiste? Harold Batiste.
Harold Batiste. Yeah.
Yeah.
That's right. Harold Batiste.
What kind of sax was he playing then?
He would play at Big Sack, what they call it, the tenor. Yeah. He had a tenor sax. He played, he played Clown that too, but he never worried much. He looked great, he was a great musician though.
Did he ever write any pieces in?

Well they tell me he writing for some big outfit in California now, you know, which you know, him and Melvin Batiste, Melvin Lestey, they had a recording studio, real, I mean, real well-equipped, yeah, right here in New Orleans. Do you remember that?
He was, Harold Batiste was with Sonny and Sheriff on the one.
That's right, that's right.
Yeah.
Yeah, he wrote some things for that.

Yeah, well, I'll keep my mouth shut. You know what I mean. Uh, about that. Uh, about that. Anyway, uh, I was wondering about the scene back then, in those times, you see, that was 1963, when I used to go to the lamppost. And then I used to go around, remember when you played that advertisement with Chester Jones? On a truck? And Austin Crawford and I were there with you? Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah. Uh, who was that saxophone player? I can't, I'll show you his picture sometime if you want to see it. I can't think of his name. I can't think. Who was that? Melvin Lestey and Harrison Verrett.
Melvin Lestey, Harrison Verrett, that's right. Uh-huh. Yeah, those boys, they, you know. Yeah, and Chester's still going.

Chester's still going, yeah. I have no idea who the saxophone player was, I've never been able to find it. Well, we got his picture, I'll show you his picture later on the front end. Yeah. You have time. Anyway, did you ever play in the Caledonia?
Oh, many times I played in the Caledonia.
What kind of place was that, nice, quiet place?

Caledonia? Uh-huh. Oh, it was beautiful, rough. Might get your head cut any time. You might be there. Go in there, hole, and come out half. Yeah? Yeah. Yeah, well during the time Professor Longhead was the start of, man. You remember old Professor Longhead? Sure. Sure. Professor of the mid that hit bald head, she ain't got no hair. All those kind of things, yeah.
Did you ever listen to him much?
Oh yeah, I listened to him at the first plenty of times. We used to work in the Caledonia together.
Uh-huh. Not at the same time.
Yeah, he'd do his show and I'd do my show.
Oh, I see, but not in the same band.
No, not in the same band, no.
No.
Well I didn't work in the Caledonia, I had a group in the Caledonia when Kit Howard had his group there.
You remember Howard, Kit Howard?

Sure, I had a group there too. Who was in your group at that time? Well I was in my group and Norman Blaze, which some of you jazz people never heard of I don't think, Eulett Jones, Herbert Jones, and Ryber Jones. Those boys there played on Boynton Street in their life.
What does Norman Blaze play?
Norman Blaze played drum. Eulett Jones played trumpet. And Ryber Jones, he was a bass player. And Hubert Jones?
And Hubert Jones, you said? No, Hubert Jones. Hubert Jones. Hubert Jones, I mean, what did he do? Yeah.
Hubert Jones, guitar man. Yeah, it was two brothers, Hubert and Ryber Jones. And during that time, the gate was the Caledonia Street.
That what?
On Decatur Street. That's where all the gigs was, look like they're on Bourbon Street now. They had more music than on Decatur Street and Charter Street than what Bourbon Street ever had.
The gigs. Yeah, that's right.

That was the street where they really had bands at, around Decatur Street, man. Or around Charter Street. See, around Franklin Avenue, towards the river, Ellison Field Avenue. Well, I mean, there's plenty of night clubs all down that way around Manaville and Charter Street.
You ever been to the H&J? H&J?
Sure, I played the H&J with Brother Cornbread. Mm-hmm.
That's the-
there a long time with Brother Cornbread playing H&J.
How old were you at that time?

Well, I was quite a young man. Well, I tell you, when I first played with Brother Cornbread, I probably would have been about 16 years old, but I mean at the H&J, I played with him during the wartime, like uh, like, like, you know, early fotties.
Was that, that would have to be before you went in the service then?

Well, I played with Brother Cornbread before I went to the service, but I mean after I went to the service in the latter part of 41, and I formed a band, they gave me, I didn't go in special service, but my company commander understood it well enough that I had talent, and he let me form a band in the service, myself, right in the club, in our outfit, like 590 Ordnance Ammunition Company, and I toured the whole Philippine Island most. We was in Manila, and I had a band, went to all the sodas, came playing music, and even played the nightclubs. They gave me, my time was off, we played the nightclubs, and gave me transportation.
Where was this? Hmm? Where was this?
In Manila.
In different places like that?
Yeah, across the seas, that's right. That was like the year 43.
Where did you get your basic training?
I got my basic training, you know, right here in Cape Livingston, Louisiana. How about that? Yeah, right out there, 17 miles on the other side of Alexander, Louisiana.
Oh yeah.

And, well, I was sent to California. That's where I went cross sea from there, Camp Stormy. And we had a time all our way going cross sea. I was playing the blues for the bars. You know, they keep pianos on them old ships, you know. Man, we played the blues going cross sea. Yes, I did.
Oh, who was at the H&J with Cornbread, you said?
I was with Cornbread at the H&J. What year did you say?
No, who was there other than you and Cornbread?
Um, I remember it's not so great, but, uh, I remember, uh, old drummer they called, uh, Jill. He used to play Bones. He was one of the old times, he used to play Bones.
Oh, you mean Jacques?
Jacques.
Yeah, I know Jacques.

Jacques, yeah, that's right. Jacques. I remember Jacques, I remember, uh, a trumpet player he had with him, with a boy, a cataract on his eye. I always wonder what happened to that boy, he was a good trumpet man.
Cataract?
Yeah, cataract on his eyes. Yeah, he played with a better call for you. Yeah.
What's Pal, uh, Palette Lane? What's Palette Lane? The Pilot Lane, however you want to say it. Pilot Lane?
Where's Pilot Lane? Yeah. Oh, Palette Lane, right back, you go back to Seminole Avenue, until it run out, Seminole Avenue runs out. And then, uh, all around Searach, uh, to Murrayview Avenue.
Yeah. Yeah.
Well, that's almost, most of the lake.
How do you pronounce it again?
Seminole, Murrayview.
Oh yeah, but how do you pronounce that place? Pilot Land?
Pilot Land, yeah. Pilot Land. Pilot Land.
Yeah. I've read about it, but I never have seen it.
Well, gee, Pilot Land was, uh, Pilot Land is way back a town then. It's way back a town, you see.
Yeah.

Like I saw them blues way back a town, well, uh, that old time, see one time, they didn't do anything back there in Polly Land, but Crawfish. You see, you didn't walk anywhere back then Crawfish, and they had old men, they had but a few families back there during that time. You see? Yeah. And I know the family, Mr. Dennis, this, this fella, they named this particular little era behind a man was named Joe Pilot Land. And he had been back there, old black man, he had been back there so long, but they named that right behind him. Ah. Joe Pilot Land. Ah. Because I mean, he was about the only family living back there, him or one or two families. You know, people go back that way hunting and catching rattlesnakes and crawfish and all that, man.
Is that rattlesnake good to eat?
Sure, man. Rattlesnake always was good to eat.
Yeah.
Eating some delicious food when you eat rattlesnake.
Yeah.
Better than chicken?
Oh, yeah.
Chicken ain't nothing but a bird.
You mentioned some other places back there, way back in town.

Oh, it's got Great Town. I know a little bit about Great Town. I've been through Great Town, you know, a few times, but that's where the other town you come from. Great Town. Yeah. But like, you see, like, Pottet Land, well, right close to Pottet Land come like Boscoville.
Yeah.
See? Boscoville. Or Lover's Land.
Lover's Land?
Yeah.
Is that just what people call it?

Well, you know where Lover's Land. That's the name of the little section right there. Where is that? That's back, if you go back in Lindenfield Street, and you come over that old pass, and you drop over that old pass, that's where it starts. Right there, you drop over that old pass, that's Lover's Land. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. That's where, uh, uh, George Lewis used to play back there, how you call it?
Sure, George Lewis, oh, George Lewis played all around in that. I guess even before I was born.

Manny's was back there, Manny's Tavern. That was in Lover's Land? Yeah, Manny's Tavern and Lover's Land. That's right. And how you call it, uh, uh, there was a restaurant back there, uh, to drive in, and I, Wallace and Raoul's was right over the Elver Pass. You remember Wallace and Raoul's?
No, I don't even thought.

It was a, uh, cement block building, and I think it, uh, I think a lot of people used to hang around there and make a drop or something. I don't know. Stuff like that. Anyway, and what about, uh, Silver City? Were you ever in Silver City?
Silver City? Remember.
Where's Boscoville?
Well, Boscoville, that's all back that way where I'm telling you about it, but Boscoville is behind those little places. It's the last thing, uh, the last thing close to the lake.
That's Gentilly and everything.
Yeah, it's way back on the other side Gentilly.
Now what about Millenburg? How far is it from Millenburg?

Well, Millenburg, well, Millenburg is like, you see, you may as well say that's by the lake, that Millenburg. You see? Now they got another place back that way, but on the other side, like Franklin Avenue, but way back. Uh-huh. I mean, Placiatum live right now. Uh, they call it the Seabrooks, but you never hardly hear people say anything about Seabrooks. No, not much anymore. Not much anymore.
That's the bridge, there's a bridge.
They named the bridge that, though, Seabrook Bridge.
Yeah, they do say that, Gentilly.

Yeah, but all that's sick with Seabrook. That's where the biggest portion of my family comes from, on my grandfather's side, the Frasiers. Great piano player like Mitchell Frasier, Alec Frasier. Alec Frasier? Yeah.
I never met him.

Yeah, well he died a young man, but he had a little age on him when he died. Played plenty of piano, but never gotten a chance to play too many nightclubs or anything like that. He taught his wife a gang of piano. Lil' Frank Moyer's sister was Alec Frasier's wife. You remember Lil' Frank Moyer?
I know him.
Lil' Daddy, they called him. He played where I'm at now at the Maison Poema.
What about Monty Land? You ever hear of that?
No, you got me on that, baby.
That's where Paul Barbering used to live, you know?
Well, yeah, well, all that before my time, you know. Like Paul, those bars, he raised before my time.
What did Alex Frasier play like? Who would you say sounded like, anybody?
Well, yeah, Alex Frasier, Father Hines, Mitchell Frasier, all them boys play around the same kind of stuff.
What's Simon?
Truthfully, they played plenty of General Rue Martin stuff.

They did, huh? Sure. That's amazing. I didn't know. That's true. Did you ever know driving them down? Who was a piano player? No, I never. No. Champion Jack, I always talked about him. You know Champion Jack Dupree? You ever know him?
Dupree.
Did you ever have a problem with him or anything?
No.
You know he's living in England now.
Yeah, he's a champion. He had a great. He's a big man now. Big blues man, Dupree. I know him now.
How did you know him?
I know anybody seen him. Some years ago, he was here around the Dewdrop.
Different place like that. What was a Dewdrop like?

Well, Dewdrop, you know, brought plenty of tracks in here. You know, like Big Joe Turner, all those kind of bars. Yeah, Dewdrop brought Donna Washington, all the people, big people there with the Dewdrop.
Yeah, they had nice paintings and everything. Remember I told you about that, huh? No. I think Johnny Don Ellis did the paintings.
Really?
Yeah. So he was there a lot. Frank Pena had it. Frank Pena, that's right. And he and Joe Turner were buddies.
Lyra Dordell. He had a hip.
Yeah, those were big names.
Big names, that's right.
Joe used to have a, I believe he had a chauffeur and a big Cadillac, big, big guy like that, as I remember it, when I'd go there. I didn't go after him.
Well sure, you know Lloyd Price, stuff from there, you know that. That's a big name, man. Lloyd Price. Fat Domino, all them bars right there. He was Dewdrop.
And who was Lollipop Jones?
Oh, he was a great comedian.
I never saw him.
Oh, he was good, Lollipop was good. He was great. He was the MC for the Dewdrops.
What did he look like?
Oh, well, he was stout. See, but no stouter than me, and about five feet level, no taller than when I was. Black.
Mustache, as I've seen. I've seen his picture.
Well, no, I don't think he wore much of a mustache. I was a dark brown skin fella, but not nothing too much to look at.
Over 200 pounds.
He was nicer looking at me, you know, that's what I'm trying to tell you. Yeah.
He weighed over 200 pounds?
Yeah, man.
And what, how did...
He started pulling our weight, I guess, on the car. He got kind of sick and he started pulling weight down.
What kind of costumes would he wear?
Oh, he wore some outgoing costumes.
Outguns?

Yeah, he really did, though. He dressed as comical, man. He dressed, you know, he had his tails on, you know, how they was made. He had, boy, he wore, you know, like two shoes together, you know. And his shoes stick out way out there, man. He was in cakes.
Would the shoes match?

He had his two, yeah, he had, well, he put on two shoes to one foot, you know. Yeah? Yeah, that's the way it was. They were all cut up and wide and everything. Then he could dance a little bit, he danced with them, you know. Oh, man, he was great. He really was great. Tell plenty of good jokes.
Do you remember any of his jokes?
No.
That must have been funny, because everybody talks about it, but I never saw him. I always missed him. He wore women's dresses and everything.
Yeah, he was something else, man.
Was he a drag queen? I don't think... Just a comedian? Or do you know?
Huh?
Was he a drag queen or a comedian or what?
I think he was a comedian.
Just a comedian. Yeah, but they used to have some real good drag queens at the dude's house.
Oh, yeah, they had many of those, yeah. They did.
They made famous ones there.
It was savage for that.
Yeah, they had some friends. Did you know Sporty Johnson?
He was an emcee I guess.
Sporter John, I know Sporter.
Is he still around?
I've been with Sporter John for years.
There used to be a lot of talent there. I never went to the Club Desire, what was that like?
Oh, the Club Desire was something big and beautiful. They brought in big things there. Club Desire was beautiful.
Sure.

It was beautiful. They brought all big attractions in Club Desire. You remember when the Fat Davin new first mate B? He was strong, going big. Well, they kept him at Club Desire. Rod Brown, that was a big man. Remember that big number that stands out today? What's that? That big number is Good Rockin' Tonight.
Oh, yeah.

And Good Rockin' At Midnight, all that. So, the boy was there. Club Desire booked all the bars. Louis Jordan, all of them at Club Desire. Joe Turner. Ivory Joe Hunter. Did you work there? I worked there many times. I didn't have with no damn band, but I worked there. Worked different little things. Big bands wouldn't come in. They used to hire all the local things, small things like me. Uh-huh. They hired them.
When did you start writing your numbers?
Well, numbers, I got that big way. I got those things right there when I got that.
Been at 20 years old. Some ideas came to me, and they still come to me.
Ideas about numbers come to me. I can't write, though. But they come to me, and how I did to capture those few air, because during the time when I'd be sleeping, and they come.
I'm going to take it.
Yeah, all right. Dave Williams, second reel. How about going? You were talking about those melodies, how they'd come to you.

Oh, yeah, they'd come to me, you know. While I'm laying back sleeping, different little melodies come to me. So I did to capture the little things I had there. At the time, I had a tape record, and I'd get up. I was my best out in writing, because I, you know, I'd not say writing, but my best way of getting my numbers, because I couldn't write. So I'd get up, and I'd tape them right fast, and I have them. But if they come to me, and I fool around there, say, well, I'll wait till I get up in the morning, and see what they're saying, you know. Well, it'd be they go away from me. I mean, I have things come to me now. But I've been kind of late on the job. It seemed like I wasn't going to never make a success in this thing, so. I just don't play melodies in the mind anymore. I just play all the melodies I hear from other people. But, it seems like things changing now, in this music world for me. I'm doing better now with it than what I ever did so far, so. I guess anything that come my way, you understand that I, you know, I'll be on the ball for it now.
You were going to ask him about the different, want me to ask him about some of the different people that I know that he played with.

Um, yeah, well, Dave, um, you were telling me downstairs, um, about some of the first groups you, you, you worked with. Um, can you say that again? Who, who, who, who were the first people who gave you jobs? And, uh, and you, you.

Well, I played jobs, I played jobs with boys like, uh, well, they were men over me, but I was quite young. They was, uh, like Euleth John. Like I first said, I played jobs with, uh, Norman Blaze, which was a drummer. I mean, he never played a job on Bowman Street before in his life. I'm more than sure, Euleth John either.
Mm-hmm.

Well, I played with those people. I played with Brother Cornbread, and many others. I even played with Bunk Johnson. I played gigs with, you know, many of them old timers way, way back, where they was in the game and then fell out of it.
Tell me when, now how old were you when you played with Bunk? Was this a?
Well, well, well, well, Bunk, this was in, uh, this was a thing right fast, did, uh, I remember, I came in on, I came in on a furlough. It was during wartime with Bunk.
Oh, with wartime, yeah.

I came in on furlough. Well, he needed piano playing right fast. Well, I was even surprised, because I knew about him, but I knew he hadn't already gotten out the game. Mm-hmm. You know, I didn't even thought he was even working anymore, because I mean, I never did see him fooling around New Orleans. Yeah, I knew he'd come out of a little country town, you know.
Yeah. Do you remember the place?

So I happened to, uh, well, I mean, I played a gig with him, I mean, uh, truthfully, I played a gig with him, in, uh, in Lashville, Lux, Lux, in Louisiana. Oh, yeah. And I, and I, I played a gig with him, in, uh, uh, right up here, around his bridge there, uh, Boutique. Uh-huh. Boutique, Louisiana, I played a gig with him. How many? How many? Playing, you know, those are the things I did with him, two, three things.
How many pieces did he have with him? Well, he had about seven pieces.

I never just stayed with him long, but it's, it was a kick to play with him old-timers like him. I played with Papa Celestine. Yeah. I never was a regular member. Yeah. But I played, you know, like they needed, I guess couldn't get through by now, so I played with those. Yeah. Which, uh, but I tell you people, like I said, that never hit Boydman Street, I played with, like, boys like Eulah Jones. Yeah. Uh, well, she's on Boydman Street now, but I remember during the time this boy, uh, playing drum with us there at the mids on Boydman, uh, Alexa. Oh, uh, Lester?
Lester? Lester, Alexa.
Lester, Alexa. Lester, Alexa. Well, I remember we had a band, a kazut band. I used to play piano, he played drum, and another boy called Albert played a kazut, was in the form of a trumpet.
I see.
You see? And we played many house parties, like two-cent house parties. Yeah. Nickel house parties like that. House be like that, be rolling. We played Saturday night fish fry.
Uh-huh.

All those kind of things, you know. When, the time when I played with those old timers, they used to take, they'd ask permission for my mother to take me on a job. Uh-huh. Then we'd make fifty cents that night, then they'd bring it home and they'd give my mother the fifty cents, and return me back to my, to my mother, you know. Yeah. Yeah, that's what they do. Yeah, I was too young to have money. Yeah. Yeah. Sometimes you make fifty cents a night. Get a good gig, you make a dollar. Mm-hmm.
Um, you were talking about, you say you went to Manila, we're in the services. Did you go anywhere else in the services? In the services?
Yeah. Well, I was in Manila.
Yeah.
And I, it was just a little zone island that the Manila's on, you understand? Yeah. I went all over to the zone island.
Did you ever go to, uh, did you ever go to Europe or did you ever go to, uh, yeah.
Yeah, I went, uh, I think I didn't go to Europe, no, but I've been to Japan, I've been to the Philippine island, I've been to Japan, I've been to the Red Land. Yeah.
Who were you in Japan with? Hmm? Who were you in Japan with?

I was in Japan with a band of myself. I played, uh, something in Japan from Manila. That's how good the army would, uh, to give us all that transportation. Mm-hmm. That's right. Didn't make no name, but I mean I was there.
What about Vietnam? How did you happen to be there?
Well, Vietnam, I went to Vietnam with Louis Contrell. Went on a five week tour in Vietnam and two weeks in Thailand.
Was it fun?

With Contrell, it wasn't much fun. Tell them about it. Kinda rough. Did you go to Saigon? Yeah, Saigon was our headquarters. That's where we landed, Saigon, that's where we lived. We stood in Saigon and we shipped out to the gate, you see, from Saigon. We take a plan to some part of Vietnam. Uh, Vietnam, then the, then the helicopter pick us up and bring us behind the hills, the mountains. And we land down where all the soldiers be. And we played two gigs a day. And we played two gigs a day. Taking a plan ride and a helicopter ride, two gigs a day. And some of the things we went so far from Saigon that we have to stay. You know, we stood overnight. Yeah. Yeah. And sometimes they get a warning that things were dangerous and things like that, you know, and they keep us. It was, oh man, it was terrible, man. And we, you see them packing up dead people in a bag, putting them on the sand, helicopter with us, packing them up. All dead people right there. And we sitting here. You know. Have to use that transportation while they could, you understand? They did, put you right along with them, you know what I mean?
Yeah.
That's the way it was, you know. A frog had a few heart attacks about it. It hurted him. Contra pretty frightened himself.
Did they shoot at you much?

Oh man, you could hear bullocks whistling around us. But I tell you what. They fooled me, you understand? Because I didn't know it was going to be like that. I thought we was going and playing, you know, a USO show. Something like that. You know. That's what I really thought it was going to be. But it was different. It really was different. Everywhere we land, the boss told us we were in danger. Everywhere we land, they fight right there. They used to tell us, the boss tell us, man, what you people doing out here, you know? They'd be glad you came, but if I was you, I would never care what we had. They'd tell us many times.
Did they have any white soldiers there? White soldiers?
Mm-hmm.
Sure.
Sure, white soldiers. Many, many, many, many white soldiers. White in color. Sure.
That's right. Went everywhere.
Everywhere they had soldiers in Vietnam, we went. We had five weeks of it, doing two jobs a day. Mm-hmm. And every job was different, so you know we went many places.
Can you cross-card? Yeah, I can cross-card.
I bet you had to out there, huh?
I could cross-card. It must have been tough piano. It was, that's mostly the thing I have to do over there.
The piano, they gave me a piano to travel with. Yeah, a folding piano. Electric?
Yeah.
They gave me a piano to travel with. Oh. Yeah. And they're taking good care of the piano. And every time I returned back to headquarters they had a man to tune it.
I guess it was no trouble. It was no trouble.
Some of the places were not going to do it. Yeah.
We got some of the places where they had pianos, you know, like upright and things, but they wasn't any good. So we cared a piano for that reason, Sam.
Sounds like New Orleans.
Yeah, we cared a piano for that reason. We ran into many bad pianos.
Oh, about cornbread, too. You were 16, you said?
No, I was only 16 when I left, played with cornbread about 8 and J.
Yeah, but earlier, before that.

Yeah, I mean, after I come out, I played with cornbread at the age of 16, but after that, I must have been in my, way in my 20s, after I come out of the service, and I played with my 8 and J. Truthfully, I did the play with him by 8 and J. after I come out, when I came out, I'd come out of the service on the furlough, and he was playing 8 and J ball in 1943 or 44, on my first furlough I was going to play with. And I did a few years, a couple of years and some months, I'd come back, I played with him again there.
What year did you get out of the service? What day?
I got out of the service in 46.
You stayed a long time?

Oh yeah, well, see, I was going to make, I was getting ready, I was going to make a career in the service. So I went in the service, early 40, like, early 40, I went in 42 February, and I stood the 46th. I re-up and everything, you know. I made a nice little rating in the service, and then after they had people, after the war was over, they had people coming in the service, wouldn't have no one push around, and they didn't know anything, you know.
Yeah.

So that made me disgusted. So if they had a little 90 dead wonder, you know. We went to school for 90 dead and get a little brass ball on their shoulder, you know. And I knew much about what I was doing, and they didn't knew, and they had to ask me, but they still wanted to dog me around. So I didn't dispute the custody, I just went on it. But during that time, you know, if you resigned and all that kind of stuff, you know, you got points where you could get out, they don't hold you. So I just, you know, told them I'd come to command, I'd like to get on out to the service. Told them I was ready.
What branch of the service were you in?
I was in the ammunition. Ordnance. Army or? Ordnance. Army or?
Ordnance.
Army, yeah. Army ammunition. Oh, I see. Army ammunition. Oh, who was in Bunk's band?
I forgot to ask you that. Do you remember? Yeah, well that would be easy to remember. What was the first job you played? My first job I played? Oh, man, that's really a fact.

The first job I played, I'll tell you what, I was about 12 years old when I played my first professional job. That was Lawrence Morell, my cousin. You remember Lawrence Morell? Oh yeah. Yeah, well Lawrence was one of the fellas, you know. Well me and Lawrence, sometime we used to hide his fellas, he used to jump. You know what I'm telling you about, what we used to do in that time, we used to play jobs around Franklin Avenue and Charters, Ellison Field and Decatur. See, all around up in there. That's where all the work was then. It wasn't all for everything. I was going to go to Hoover Street.
What about Toker? Did you ever work with Toker? Lawrence Toker? Oh yeah.

I'm glad you mention that. I'm sure glad you mention that. I forgot about him Toker. Yeah, that man hired me on a plenty little thing. Toker the trumpet player on a little Toker, sure. Yeah, I did a plenty thing with Toker. I know there was somebody I was there. I don't know it was somebody I was trying to think about. That's right.
What about, let's see, we got to Club Desire, did they have any acts there? Club Desire?
Yeah, Club Desire had some acts like, like the Doudrop, you know, some of them people wearing dresses and things.
Did they have dancers ever?
Yeah, they had dancers, they had beautiful dance flow.
I mean on stage, did they ever have anybody who did a tap dance?
Yeah, they had dance shows.
Who would be in those shows?
Well, the same people like, when they wasn't at the Doudrop, they was there.
I just wondered if they had any big name dancers.
Yeah, you don't know, yeah.
Did you ever see Peg Leg Bates? Oh yeah, man, something. Did you ever work with him?
No, I never worked with him.
What about Butter Beans and Suze here? I don't know. Big Meat, Markham, any of those people?
I never worked with those people.
They never didn't have that stuff at the, did they come to town?
Butter Beans and Suze, sure they came to, when they had the Palace Theatre, Dorthy and what that was there was, the Piavels, Butter Beans and Suze, the Palace Theatre.
The Pig Meat was there.
The Pig Meat, all those people come back. I was a kid, I was not a kid, I remember that.
Yeah. Yeah, because I wondered what kind of comedians I had in these places.
Good, good old childhood man.
Dave, you once mentioned you were playing in a place, and Francis Domino was playing in the same place before he was discovered, before he made a hit. Tell me about this, where was this place?
Well, they called it The Hideaway.
The Hideaway.
Yeah, Fat had a band and I was there, a band, had two bands.
How many, how big were the bands?

Two of them small bands, like four or five people. Yeah. And Fat and I were working in the same place, just working. Yeah. And one night, fella come through there, I wasn't working. I'd say I'd probably been just as lucky as Fat, you know, if I'd been there. And made Fat been made ever since.
Where was The Hideaway?
The Hideaway was back, oh, way back in the Night War, there, they read that, that, uh, uh, on Louisa, back on the wheels around Pida.
I came past.
Uh, way back on the wheels around Pida.
Is that around the, is that across the canal? Yeah.
Across the Florida Canal? That, that, that's, uh.
Florida Avenue Canal?
Yeah, that's, uh. Across Florida Mall. Yeah, that's Florida, North Florida Mall? Yeah. All that cross there, that, that's where they got the, uh, they call it the Desire Project now.
Yeah. They ripped all that out?
Right, that's how they tore it down, because they would, they built the Desire Project. That's how the people had to, you know, get rid of their nightclubs.
Well, who did you make records with?

Records? Yeah. Did I make any records? Okay. Yeah, I did, uh, Kit Harvin. Uh, yeah. Nope. I didn't do too much recording. It's Freddie Coleman. Yeah, you made it. Yeah, I read some. Remember I already showed you that book? Yeah, Freddie Coleman, I did something with some people, I forgot, beat two, three times.
Yeah, I remember. Oh yeah.
Yeah, Smiling Joe, that's right.
We can check in Don Stagg and, uh, and Charlie Crump. Okay. Yeah. Who was in Smiling Joe's group when you recorded?
It was, it was me, I think.
I never heard those. Who had? Yeah.
Yeah, me, uh, Clem, I think it was Clem Trevilland, uh, Toma Jefferson.
Oh, yeah, that's the same band as Freddie Coleman.
That was the same band as Freddie Coleman. Yeah. Where were they? We were working at the, uh, Sidney Villa place. Remember Sidney Villa? Yeah.
Mardi Gras Lounge.
Mardi Gras Lounge, yeah, that's right. Yeah.
And Smiling Joe would use, yeah?
Smiling Joe would there, Leslie Miles. Uh-huh.
Oh, we'll have to check all that out, you know? Uh-huh. What about people like, uh, Red Caillou? Did you ever listen to him?
Red Caillou Toots?

Not, not Red Toots. Oh. Red Caillou. Red Caillou. I don't know if you ever heard, he may have left town, he left a long time ago, I never met him. What about Friday Ford, you ever hear of him? Uh-uh. Little Willie Forrest?
No, man.
Little Willie, you didn't know Little Willie? Got killed in the bathroom?
Oh, Little Willie, the pianist. Yeah. Yeah. Let me get those people out of his name. Yeah, yeah, that's right.
Was he any good?

Oh, he was a good piano man. Little Willie, sure man. Yeah, I used to admire him, he's playing, you know. Mm-hmm. During that time, uh, a friend of mine was playing, he did, and I called him Bunnell Sanago. Mm-hmm. And I'm catching to meet during that time and see who could outplay one another, you know. Mm-hmm. I had Little Willie, Bunnell Sanago, Mitchell Frazier, Simon Frazier, all in the bubble. I was under those parts, and they was playing too much for me. And they'll meet, man, and on Mondays, and tell me about the red beans and rice and plenty wine.
Yeah.
Plenty fine women.
And you used to hear?
Best piano player get the finest woman, you know. And plenty fun.
Uh-huh.
Best musician get treated the best, you know. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Wow. That's the way it was. Oh, well, yeah.
Best times have gone, man.
Yeah, man. Uh, what's about Steve, you remember Steve Lloyd?
I never met him.
Yeah, he was a great man, too.
Do you remember him? Sure.
It was back then, Little Willie in that time. Little Willie in that time. A little older than Little Willie in there, but he was right there, calling Steve Lloyd.
Did you sing any of his numbers?
Any piano he played, man. Yeah.
What did Kid Clayton play on? Kid Clayton play on piano. I never heard him play.
Kid Clayton. I never know if Kid Clayton would play piano. They say he could play. I thought he played. I thought he was a piano or trumpet man.
I heard he played like sheep.
Yeah, he probably played a little blues.
Well, Fernandez plays piano too. And Albert Walters plays piano.
Sure, Albert Walters, that's right.
But I never heard him much. I heard him a little bit on the piano. Yeah.
Yeah, but they tell me he was a real great, he was a piano man, Fernandez.
Oh, you didn't tell me much about Miele Barnes.

Well, Miele, I knew Miele all my life. Miele related to me. But I never played with him or, you know, and the only time I really got to really him, Miele, been a nice fellow all the days, but the only time I got to him was, you know, when he's the preservation, all opened up and all that, you know. But like Miele, Paul Barnes, all that's my relatives, Saif Frazier, Lawrence Marrero, all that's family. Very close too. Sisters and brothers, children, you know.
Yeah.
Very close.
But what about George Lutz? Did you have an album here?
Oh, George, sure. I know George. He's a good friend of George all my young life. I played gigs with George. I know George. Yes, indeed.
Where did you play the gigs with George?

I played gigs all around New Orleans with George. George played the Caldone. He played gigs. He played gigs. Like I was telling you, down around Franklin Avenue and Charters, all around there, before he'd come before they played, Boehme Street. All around Decatur Street, Charter Street. Manavill and Charters. All around St. Rock Street. Those neighborhoods, you'd have many neighborhoods, many neighborhoods, ballrooms during them times that had music. Yeah. You know? Neighborhood ballroom that had music. Yeah. And then you got so now, you got to get a job on Boehme Street, but you used to go play at the corner of your house, man. You know what I'm talking about? And a giant or something like that, too. An old giant one's talking about.
Early thirties. And I guess even where before that time, you know. Poison River Hall was blooming then. Remember the old Poison River Hall?
I know where it is.
Yeah, very near that hall, the Poison River Hall, all those old halls, things was happening with them then. People give plenty of things they call bonkers.
Whereabouts was Perseverance Hall?
Well, that's around 1600 Block Virid Street between Sempernard Avenue and then that street.
Uh, yeah. Now, uh, San Jacinto was gone.
Sure, Jacinto's all the more. He'd commonly hall, Jacinto's all that.
How many of them did you work in?

I worked in all of them. I worked Jacinto's Hall, Jacinto's Hall, I worked those places. I mean many times, I played many dances either. I remember one time, me and my little band, I don't say I ain't got a name, but I had a little band that all the people where I come from, like the Sempernard, they had clubs and everything they give, they hired me. And they give them in the Comedy Hall and they give them in the the hall I just called Virid Street there, Perseverance Hall, and they hired me. You know? I formed a band and played those things. Many things I played, many things. I played picnets. I wanted you to give picnets every Sunday and all that, you know? I played all those things. I played much, much music in my life. Why did I get to be a man without any kind of name? That's the truth. I had more connection playing music in the city of New Orleans. I believe in any band, like I'm talking about the club, including like Lewis Contra, all them people, all those kind of people. But somehow they made a man for themselves. But me, I played more music. I think I played more jobs than all those people because I mean, those people played jobs, you understand, like Bourbon Street.
Yeah. But you were working all over town.
That's right. But I played jobs all over the city, neighborhood ballrooms, everywhere I played jobs, you know? Like that.
Um, what about fish fries? What's the fish fries?
Oh, we played fish fry down. Plenty of fish fry. Oh, man. That's good days, fish fry. And what made it so nice, you know what I mean? You hear the police come and you have to jump the back fence.
How come were you making too much noise or something?

Well, people didn't get fish fries and some of them would use permits. You know? I mean, they have to go sign again. Oh, you have to have to come. Yeah. And some people take up nerves and have them without the permit. So those who give them without the permit, you just have to jump the back fence when the man was coming, you know? Yeah. I remember when I was a kid, I used to play things they called speakeasies. Yeah. You know? I would do them for liquor time. We didn't sell no liquor. What they called that prohibition. And we'd get in, they used to sell that old bad wine and stuff. They have a piano in there. How they did the name of the thing, speakeasy, because every time like you or I be drinking, when we get low loud and somebody, shh, speakeasy. I tell you to speakeasy, you know? Don't make too much noise. Speak low, you know? Yeah. Say, speakeasy, man. Speakeasy.
I wonder how that started.

Yeah, that's how that started. Which I'm just telling the part that I know, but I guess it's been going on before my time, with my dad and them, you know? I just come up and find it, you know what I mean? Yeah, yeah. I'm not trying to create anything. I just come up and find those things in my time. When I come up, it was happening.
Did you ever play a harmonica or a...
Yeah, I play a harmonica. I love to play a harmonica. Oh yeah? Yeah. You still play it? Yeah, yeah. I play harmonica. Nice. I like to play harmonica. Tell Allison. 된된된

segments.title: Interview opening and why the Eagle session was made
segments.summary: Name, date and setting are stated; Williams explains the recording was made with his small band and Poirier for the little Eagle company.

segments.title: Janellis and the Eagle label's fate
segments.summary: Eagle was a small New Orleans company near Little Woods owned by Janellis, who died before the records were released.

segments.title: Recording at Janellis's home
segments.summary: Mic check, then the session in Janellis's house; he believed Williams deserved a break and was friendly with him.

segments.title: Session personnel and how Lloyd became a drummer
segments.summary: Musicians on the session; Lloyd took up drums at the Lamp Post on Bourbon; Janellis engineered in his front room.

segments.title: Leroy's patio, Frog, George Williams and Blanche Thomas
segments.summary: Williams recalls musicians who worked with him at Leroy's and the Blue Angel, and Blanche Thomas as his vocalist.

segments.title: Playhouse and Harold Batiste
segments.summary: Working the Playhouse with Harold Batiste, his tenor sax, and later California writing and a New Orleans studio.

segments.title: The 1963 Lamp Post scene and Chester Jones's truck
segments.summary: Interviewer recalls 1963, the Chester Jones advertising truck and an unidentified saxophonist.

segments.title: The Caledonia and Professor Longhair
segments.summary: The Caledonia was beautiful but rough; Longhair and Williams did separate shows there.

segments.title: Group at the Caledonia and Decatur Street music
segments.summary: Williams' group with Kid Howard's, the Jones brothers and Norman Blaze; Decatur and Charter Streets had more music than Bourbon.

segments.title: Playing the H&J with Brother Cornbread
segments.summary: He played with Cornbread at 16 and again during the war; he formed a band at his Ordnance company after going in late 1941.

segments.title: Service band in Manila and basic training
segments.summary: He toured the Philippines with a service band, trained at Camp Livingston and played blues on the ship crossing.

segments.title: Who played at the H&J
segments.summary: He recalls the drummer Jacques, who played bones, and a trumpeter with a cataract.

segments.title: Pilot Land, Boscoville and Lover's Land
segments.summary: Geography of the back-of-town lake districts, how Pilot Land got its name and local crawfish and rattlesnake talk.

segments.title: George Lewis, Manny's Tavern and Millenburg
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about places where George Lewis played, Silver City, Boscoville and Millenburg.

segments.title: The Frasier family and piano styles
segments.summary: His grandfather's family from Seabrook: Alec and Mitchell Frasier, their piano style, and Lil Frank Moyer.

segments.title: Champion Jack Dupree and the Dewdrop Inn
segments.summary: Dupree, Big Joe Turner, Lloyd Price and Fats Domino around the Dewdrop.

segments.title: Lollipop Jones, the Dewdrop comedian
segments.summary: Description of Lollipop Jones, the Dewdrop MC: his size, costumes, dancing and jokes, and the drag shows.

segments.title: Sporty Johnson and the Club Desire
segments.summary: Williams knew Sporty Johnson; Club Desire booked big acts and hired local small players like him.

segments.title: How his melodies come to him
segments.summary: He started writing numbers around 20; since he cannot write notation, he tapes tunes that come in his sleep.

segments.title: First jobs, Bunk Johnson and the kazoo band
segments.summary: Early jobs with Norman Blaze and Cornbread, a wartime gig with Bunk Johnson, Papa Celestine, the kazoo band and house parties.

segments.title: Service travel to the Philippines and Japan
segments.summary: He went to Manila and Japan with his own band, with army transportation.

segments.title: Vietnam tour with Louis Cottrell
segments.summary: A five-week USO-style tour from Saigon, two gigs a day by plane and helicopter, in danger and amid the dead.

segments.title: The folding piano and bad pianos
segments.summary: He was given a folding piano that was tuned at headquarters since local pianos were poor.

segments.title: Years in the Army and discharge
segments.summary: Clarifying Cornbread dates; he entered in February 1942, left in 1946 disgusted with promotions, in Army ammunition ordnance.

segments.title: First professional job and Lawrence Toca
segments.summary: At about twelve he played with his cousin Lawrence Marrero around Franklin and Charters; also jobs with trumpeter Toca.

segments.title: Club Desire acts, dancers and comedians
segments.summary: Dance shows and acts; Peg Leg Bates, Butterbeans and Susie and Pigmeat at the Palace Theatre.

segments.title: The Hideaway and Fats Domino
segments.summary: He and Fats Domino worked small bands at the Hideaway before Domino was discovered; location lost to the Desire Project.

segments.title: Recordings with Smiling Joe and Freddie Coleman
segments.summary: His few records, with Smiling Joe's band that worked at the Mardi Gras Lounge.

segments.title: Little Willie, piano contests and other pianists
segments.summary: Admired pianists like Little Willie, Mitchell Frazier and Steve Lloyd; Monday piano contests; others discussed.

segments.title: Relatives and George Lewis gigs
segments.summary: Miele Barnes, Lawrence Marrero and others are family; he played neighborhood gigs with George Lewis.

segments.title: Perseverance Hall and neighborhood ballrooms
segments.summary: Halls like Perseverance and Jacinto's where he played dances and picnics; he played more jobs than famous names.

segments.title: Fish fries, speakeasies and harmonica
segments.summary: Fish fries without permits, speakeasies in prohibition and the origin of the term, then a harmonica question.
